t: American Amber Lager
d: The lager for people who want a bit more bread in the glass, without giving up the clean finish.
x: Think of a standard lager, then add a slice of toast. That is the amber lager in a sentence. Brewers take a clean lager base and lean on crystal and Munich-type malts for colour and a gentle caramel note, then keep the hops polite so the malt can lead. It finishes drier than its colour suggests, because a cold, slow lager fermentation strips out the fruity esters an ale would leave behind.  The style grew up in American brewpubs and regional breweries in the 1980s and 1990s, as a step up from pale mass-market lager that still felt familiar. It borrows from the Vienna and Märzen tradition but is looser about it: some versions carry a light citrus or floral hop note from American varieties, others stay strictly malty. What keeps it honest is balance. A good one is easy to drink by the pint, with enough malt to stand up to food and enough bitterness that the second glass does not feel sweet.

t: Munich Dunkel
d: Dark in the glass, gentle on the tongue: a lager that tastes of bread crust, not roast coffee.
x: Dunkel means dark. That is about all it shares with stout. The colour comes mainly from Munich malt, kilned hotter than pale malt so it carries a deep bread-crust and toasted-nut flavour. Brewers add only a small amount of dark malt, so there is little roast bitterness. The result tastes like the crust of a rye loaf or a well-baked bun, with a whisper of chocolate at most.  This was the everyday beer of Munich and the Bavarian countryside for centuries, long before pale lagers took over the beer halls. Traditional brewers used a decoction mash, boiling part of the mash and returning it, which deepens the malt character and gives that rounded, almost toffee-like richness. Hops are German noble varieties, used for balance rather than aroma. A good dunkel is soft, malty and surprisingly easy to drink. If yours tastes burnt or acrid, the brewer has drifted towards schwarzbier or used too much roasted grain.

t: Märzen / Oktoberfest
d: Brewed in spring, drunk in autumn: the toasty amber lager behind every Oktoberfest menu.
x: Märzen is named after March, the last month Bavarian brewers could safely brew before summer heat spoiled fermentations. They made it a little stronger, lagered it cold in caves through the summer and drank the last of it in autumn, which is how it became tied to Oktoberfest. Today the name covers a rich amber lager with a lot of Munich and Vienna malt, giving toast, light caramel and a bready sweetness.  It is fuller and a touch stronger than a standard lager, yet it should finish clean and fairly dry so you can drink a litre mug without tiring. Hop bitterness is moderate and German in character, herbal rather than fruity. One wrinkle: the beer served in Munich's festival tents today is usually a paler, lighter festbier, while the deeper amber Märzen survives more in export bottles and in craft breweries abroad. Both share the same idea, malt-led and smooth, built for long sessions with food.

t: Schwarzbier
d: A black beer that drinks like a lager: roast on the nose, light and crisp on the finish.
x: Schwarzbier is the beer that breaks the rule that dark means heavy. Pour one and it looks like a stout, nearly black with a tan head. Drink it and it is lighter, drier and crisper than most people expect, closer to a pilsner in body than to anything from Ireland. The colour comes from dehusked roasted malts, which give dark chocolate and coffee notes with very little of the acrid bite that husks bring.  Its home is Thuringia and Saxony in eastern Germany, where black lagers have been brewed for centuries. Unlike dunkel, which is all bread crust and softness, schwarzbier has a firmer bitterness and a drier, more roasty edge, but it should never taste burnt. The lager yeast and long cold conditioning keep it clean. For a brewer it is a test of restraint: enough roast to be interesting, little enough that you could drink two on a warm afternoon.

t: Vienna Lager
d: Amber lager at its most elegant: a light toast, a dry finish and nothing out of place.
x: Vienna lager started in 1841, when Anton Dreher in Vienna paired a lighter, more carefully kilned malt with the new cold-fermenting lager yeast. The malt that took the city's name is the heart of the beer. It sits between pale and Munich malt, giving a gentle toast and a light, almost honeyed sweetness rather than heavy caramel.  The style faded in Austria but found a second home in Mexico, carried there by Austrian-born brewers in the late nineteenth century. It survives in several darker Mexican lagers. In the glass it is reddish amber, clear and clean. Compared with Märzen, it is lighter in body, drier and a little more bitter, so it feels brisker. Compared with American amber lager, it is more restrained, with no citrusy hops. A good Vienna lager is a quiet beer that rewards attention: toast, a soft malt middle, a firm dry finish.

t: Belgian Blonde Ale
d: Golden, gently sweet and quietly strong: the friendliest door into Belgian beer.
x: The Belgian blonde is the abbey brewers' crowd-pleaser. It is golden, soft and a little sweet, with the fruity and spicy notes that Belgian yeast strains produce: pear, a touch of banana, a hint of clove or pepper. The malt is mostly pale pilsner malt, sometimes with a little sugar added to the boil so the beer finishes drier and lighter than its strength suggests.  The style became popular in the twentieth century as abbey breweries added a pale beer to sit beside their darker dubbels. It is less spicy and less dry than a tripel and noticeably less hoppy, with a softer, rounder middle. The alcohol is real, usually between six and eight per cent, but it should be smooth rather than hot. What you are tasting is mostly the yeast. Fermented a little warm, Belgian yeast throws esters and phenols that make the beer taste far more complex than its short ingredient list.

t: Belgian Dubbel
d: A brown abbey ale that tastes of raisins, plums and dark toffee, with a dry, warming finish.
x: Dubbel is the brown ale of the Trappist and abbey tradition. Its modern form took shape at Westmalle in the mid-nineteenth century and spread to other monasteries and then to commercial abbey breweries. The colour and much of the flavour come from dark candi syrup, a caramelised beet sugar that gives raisin, plum and dark toffee notes, along with Munich and some Special B malt.  The Belgian yeast adds dried fruit and a soft spice, so the whole beer tastes something like a fruit cake that has been dried out. It should not be heavy or syrupy. The sugar ferments out, leaving a medium body and a surprisingly dry finish with a gentle warmth from the alcohol. Hops stay low, there only to keep things in balance. Roast is absent; if a dubbel tastes of coffee or burnt toast, it has wandered away from the style. Strength usually sits around six to seven and a half per cent.

t: Belgian Golden Strong Ale
d: Looks like a lager, drinks like champagne and is often nearly as strong as wine. Respect it.
x: The golden strong ale is a trick played on the eye. It looks pale and bright, like a pilsner, but it can be as strong as a light wine. The style took its modern shape around 1970, when Duvel Moortgat turned its strong ale pale to answer the fashion for golden lager: very light pilsner malt, a good dose of plain sugar to thin the body and a vigorous Belgian yeast.  The sugar is the secret. It ferments away completely, so the beer finishes very dry and light despite all that alcohol. Pear, apple and a little citrus come from the yeast, along with a peppery spice. The hops are more noticeable than in a blonde, adding a fine bitterness and a herbal or spicy note that keeps the finish crisp. Carbonation is high, sometimes close to sparkling wine. It is less sweet than a tripel, though the two are close cousins and many drinkers confuse them.

t: Belgian Pale Ale
d: The everyday Belgian: amber, biscuity and moderate, made for drinking rather than sipping.
x: Not every Belgian beer is strong and spicy. The Belgian pale ale is the everyday café beer of Flanders and Antwerp, a copper-coloured ale of around five per cent that sits comfortably beside a meal. It took its modern shape in the early twentieth century, partly influenced by British pale ales, as Belgian brewers looked for an answer to imported beers.  Compared with an English pale ale it carries more toasty, biscuity malt and a gentle fruit and spice from the yeast, though far less than in a blonde or tripel. Pear and orange peel sit in the background, with a soft pepper note. Hops give a moderate, clean bitterness and a light herbal or earthy aroma. The body is medium-light and the finish is dry and easy. It is a modest beer by Belgian standards. That is the point: it shows how well Belgian yeast works when nobody is trying to show off.

t: Belgian Quadrupel
d: The abbey family's heavyweight: dark fruit, burnt sugar and warmth, made for slow evenings.
x: Quadrupel is the largest of the abbey family, a dark, rich and strong ale that often runs from ten to twelve per cent. The name was popularised by La Trappe in the Netherlands in the early 1990s, but the style covers a wider family of Belgian dark strong ales that monasteries and abbey brewers had made for decades.  Expect a deep mahogany beer with raisin, fig, plum and dark cherry, layered over caramel and burnt sugar from dark candi syrup. Belgian yeast adds a peppery or clove-like spice and a little banana. Despite the strength it should not taste like a syrup; the sugar ferments well, keeping the body full but not cloying. The alcohol should warm rather than burn. Bitterness is moderate and mostly there for balance. Think of it as a dubbel with everything turned up. These beers age gracefully, picking up sherry and port notes over a year or two in a cool cellar.

t: Saison
d: A bone-dry farmhouse ale where the yeast does most of the talking.
x: Saison started as the beer of Wallonian farms, brewed in the cooler months and kept for the people working the fields in summer. Every farm had its own version, so the style has always been loose around the edges. What ties modern saisons together is the yeast. Saison strains are some of the hungriest in brewing: they chew through sugars most ale yeasts leave behind, which is why a good one finishes with a final gravity near 1.002 and almost no sweetness at all.  That yeast also throws pepper, clove and a fruity note somewhere between pear and orange peel. Hops sit behind it, usually earthy or spicy rather than tropical. Some brewers add coriander, ginger or black pepper, but the best examples get their spice from fermentation alone. The finish is dry, prickly and a little tart. It makes you want the next sip. A saison fermented warm, often well above 25 °C, is behaving exactly as it should, which is one reason Indian brewers like the style.

t: Belgian Tripel
d: Golden, strong and surprisingly dry. It drinks lighter than its 8 to 9 percent.
x: Tripel is the strong golden ale of the Belgian abbey tradition, brought to its modern form at Westmalle in the 1930s. It looks like a pale lager and carries the strength of a fortified wine, which is exactly why it catches people out. The trick is sugar. Brewers add plain white or candi sugar to a pale malt base. The yeast turns it into alcohol without leaving body behind. The result is a beer that sits around 8 to 9 percent but finishes dry and almost crisp.  The flavour is mostly yeast and malt in balance. Expect banana, pear and orange from the esters, a peppery, clove-like spice, soft honeyed malt and a firm but quiet bitterness from noble hops. Alcohol shows as a gentle warmth, never as solvent or heat. A hot, boozy tripel usually means fermentation ran away without temperature control. A good one is lively, bottle conditioned and dangerous in the most polite way.

t: Bock
d: A strong dark lager that is all about bread crust and toasted malt.
x: Bock traces back to Einbeck in northern Germany, a medieval brewing town whose strong beer was prized well beyond its walls. When Munich brewers copied it, the Bavarian pronunciation of Einbeck slid into ein Bock. The name stuck, along with the goat that still turns up on labels. Today's bock is a Munich creation: a strong lager with a long, cold maturation that rounds off any rough edges.  The flavour is malt from start to finish. Munich and Vienna malts give toasted bread crust, light caramel and a hint of nuttiness, often with the rich, Maillard depth that traditional decoction mashing produces. Hops are there only to keep the sweetness honest, so bitterness is moderate and hop aroma is barely noticeable. There should be no roast, no coffee and no fruity ale esters. Clean lager fermentation and weeks of lagering near freezing give a smooth beer whose strength shows as warmth, not burn.

t: Doppelbock
d: Liquid bread from Munich. Rich, strong and smooth, with names that end in -ator.
x: Doppelbock was first brewed by the Paulaner monks in Munich, who needed something nourishing to get through the Lenten fast. Their beer, later sold as Salvator, set the pattern. Many doppelbocks since have taken names ending in -ator as a nod to it. Despite the name, it is not double the strength of a bock. It is simply a bigger, richer version.  The flavour is dense malt: dark bread, toffee, dried fruit such as raisin and plum and, in darker versions, a touch of chocolate without any harsh roast. Hops play a supporting role. A long, cold lagering smooths the beer so the alcohol feels warm and gentle rather than hot. Paler versions exist, closer to gold than brown, but most are deep amber to dark brown. A good doppelbock is sweet in the mouth yet finishes clean enough to invite another sip.

t: Maibock
d: The pale, hoppier bock. Strong enough to warm you, bright enough for spring.
x: Maibock is the pale member of the bock family, brewed for the spring tapping season in Bavaria, hence the name May bock. You will also see it called helles bock. Take a bock, swap most of the Munich malt for Pilsner malt, raise the hops a little and you are close.  The result tastes of fresh bread and honey rather than toast and caramel, with a clean, firm bitterness and a little spicy or floral hop aroma from German varieties. It carries 6 to 7 percent alcohol or more, but it is drier and more drinkable than its darker cousins. The alcohol hides well. Like any bock, it needs long, cold lagering, which strips away the sulphur and rough edges of young lager and leaves a beer that is bright, smooth and clean. If it tastes buttery or fruity, something went wrong in the fermenter.

t: Weizenbock
d: A hefeweizen with the strength and richness of a bock. Banana bread in a glass.
x: Weizenbock is what happens when Bavarian wheat beer meets bock strength. Schneider in Munich set the template in the early 1900s with a dark, strong wheat beer. Pale versions followed later. The recipe is a hefeweizen scaled up: at least half wheat malt, the same top-fermenting weissbier yeast and enough extra malt to reach 7 to 9 percent.  That yeast is the star. It gives banana and clove. At this strength those notes deepen into banana bread, baked apple, plum and raisin. Dark versions add caramel and a light chocolate edge, while pale ones stay closer to honey and fresh bread. Hops barely register. The wheat gives a soft, fluffy texture and a big head. The high carbonation keeps a rich beer from feeling heavy. Fermentation temperature decides the balance: warmer pushes banana, cooler pushes clove. Brewers tune it to taste.

t: American Brown Ale
d: Chocolate and caramel with a proper American hop bite. Brown ale with its sleeves rolled up.
x: American brown ale grew out of the US homebrew scene in the 1980s, when brewers took the English brown ale and gave it the treatment they gave everything: more malt, more hops, more of each. It stays drinkable, though. Think of it as the space between an American pale ale and a porter.  The base is caramel and chocolate malt, which gives toffee, cocoa, toasted nuts and a touch of light roast without the coffee bitterness of a stout. On top sit American hops, usually citrusy or piney varieties such as Cascade or Centennial, both in the aroma and in a firm, dry bitterness. The best examples keep malt and hops in balance so neither shouts. Clean American ale yeast keeps the fruitiness low, which lets the chocolate and hop notes stand clear. It finishes drier than its English cousin and a little more bitter.

t: English Brown Ale
d: Nutty, toffee-sweet and easy-going. A pub beer that never tries too hard.
x: English brown ale is a working pub beer from the north and the Midlands of England. The northern versions, of which Newcastle Brown is the famous one, are drier and paler. The southern versions are darker and sweeter, closer to a strong mild. Both share the same idea: malt first, low strength, easy to drink by the pint.  Crystal and a little chocolate malt give toffee, biscuit, caramel and a nutty character often compared to hazelnut. Hops are English varieties such as Fuggles or East Kent Goldings, used for balance rather than aroma, so bitterness is low and earthy. English ale yeast adds a soft fruitiness, a hint of dried fruit or apple. There is no harsh roast. The finish is gently sweet to medium-dry. A good English brown is quiet and well put together. Its pleasure comes from that balance.

t: English Mild
d: Big malt flavour at small strength. The beer you drink when you want to keep talking.
x: Mild is one of England's oldest pub styles. In the past mild meant young, fresh beer as opposed to aged and soured stock, not low strength. Through the twentieth century it became the everyday ale of industrial towns, brewed weaker and darker. Today most milds sit between 3 and 4 percent.  The skill lies in getting real flavour into so little alcohol. Brewers use crystal, chocolate and sometimes brown malt to give caramel, toffee, cocoa, light coffee and dried fruit. They mash warm to leave some unfermentable sugar for body, so a good mild never tastes thin or watery. Hops are kept low and English, there for balance. English ale yeast adds a little fruit. Most milds are dark, but pale versions exist. The best ones are served fresh on cask with low carbonation. They are made to be drunk by the pint over a long evening.

t: Cream Ale
d: An ale that wants to be a lager. Crisp, clean and very easy on a hot day.
x: Cream ale is an American invention from the late 1800s, when ale brewers in the north-east were losing drinkers to the new pale lagers. Their answer was a light, clean ale, often fermented warm and then stored cold, sometimes blended with lager. Despite the name, there is no cream in it. The creaminess is mostly in the marketing.  It tastes of light, sweetish grain with a corn or rice character, very low hop aroma and a low bitterness. Corn gives a faint sweetness, rice keeps it drier and crisper. A cool fermentation with a clean ale yeast keeps fruitiness to a whisper, so the beer drinks almost like a lager, with a touch more roundness in the middle. It is pale, highly carbonated and refreshing. A good cream ale has no flaws to hide behind, which makes it a better test of a brewery than any double IPA.

t: California Common
d: A lager yeast made to work in ale weather. The beer is better for it.
x: California Common starts with a problem we know well in India: brewing lager without enough cold. Brewers in nineteenth century San Francisco had lager yeast but little refrigeration, so they fermented it warm in wide, shallow vessels and let the bay air do what it could. The result kept some lager cleanliness and picked up a gentle fruitiness that a cold lager never shows.  In the glass it is amber to light copper, with toasty, bready malt and a firm bitterness that lands harder than you expect from the colour. The signature is the hop: Northern Brewer, which smells of mint, pine and old wood rather than citrus. Finish is dry and a little grainy. It sits between an amber lager and a pale ale and borrows the best manners of each.  The trick is the yeast strain. A good California lager strain stays clean at 14 to 18 °C, where most lager yeasts would throw sulphur and solvent. Pick the wrong one and you have a muddled amber ale.

t: Biere de Garde
d: The farmhouse beer that was brewed in winter and kept for the summer harvest.
x: Biere de garde means beer for keeping. Farm breweries in French Flanders, on the border with Belgium, brewed it in the cooler months and held it in cellars for the warm season when brewing was risky. That long, cold rest is what shapes it: the beer comes out smooth and rounded, with the rough edges of fermentation worn away.  Expect a malt led beer. The common versions are amber or brown, with toffee, bread crust and a faint cellar earthiness some drinkers call musty in a good way. Blond versions exist and are a little drier and spicier. Hops stay in the background, a herbal note rather than a bitter one. Strength runs from table beer to something closer to a strong ale, so read the label.  What separates it from a Belgian saison is restraint. Saison is peppery, dry and yeast driven. Biere de garde is clean, malty and patient, often fermented with ale yeast at the cool end or with lager yeast, then lagered for weeks. It is a beer for the table more than the bar.

t: Altbier
d: Dusseldorf's answer to lager: an ale that drinks like one, with more bite.
x: Alt means old. The name points at the older way of brewing: top fermenting ale yeast, used in Dusseldorf long after most of Germany switched to lager. The Dusseldorf brewers kept the yeast and borrowed the cold. They ferment cool, around 13 to 19 °C, then lager the beer for weeks near freezing.  The result is copper to brown, very clean and more bitter than its colour suggests. Munich malt gives a bready, nutty base, sometimes a little toasted. Noble German hops add a spicy, peppery bitterness that runs to a dry finish. There is almost no fruit from the yeast. If you like a brown ale but find it sweet, or like lager but want more flavour, this is the beer.  In the old town of Dusseldorf it is served in small, straight glasses and replaced as soon as you empty one. The bitterness is the point. A soft, sweet altbier is a brown ale wearing the wrong label.

t: Kolsch
d: Cologne's pale, delicate ale, brewed with lager discipline and gone in four sips.
x: Kolsch is the local beer of Cologne. In Germany the name is protected for brewers in and around that city. It is an ale, fermented with top fermenting yeast, but cool, then cold conditioned like a lager. That gives a beer which looks like a pale lager and tastes softer and a little fruitier.  It is pale straw to light gold and brilliantly clear. The malt is soft and bready, like a fresh white loaf. Hops are gentle and herbal, never citrus. The yeast leaves a faint fruit, a hint of pear or white wine, that you notice and then lose. The finish is dry and short.  In Cologne it comes in a thin 200 ml glass, the stange, carried round on a ring tray and refilled until you put a beer mat on top. The small glass is practical: Kolsch is fragile and tastes best in the first minutes. A Kolsch that tastes of sulphur or of nothing at all has been rushed. That is the commonest fault you will meet.

t: Irish Red Ale
d: A quiet, malty pub beer whose red colour comes from a pinch of roast, not from sugar.
x: Irish red is a modest beer. That is its charm. It is a session ale from Irish pubs, low in strength, made to drink in rounds. The red comes from a small amount of roasted barley, the same grain that turns a stout black, used here in tiny amounts so it colours the beer and adds a dry, toasty edge.  Expect toffee and biscuit up front, a little buttered toast, then that dry roast at the end. Hops are low and earthy, there to balance rather than to show off. Some versions carry a touch of butterscotch from the yeast; in small amounts that is part of the style, in large amounts it is a fault.  The difference from an American amber is the hops. An American amber has citrus and pine and more bitterness. The Irish beer is all about malt and finishes drier than you think. Many commercial Irish reds lean sweet; a good one finishes clean enough to have a second.

t: American IPA
d: Clear, bitter and loud with American hops, the beer that defined craft for a generation.
x: American IPA took the English idea of a strong, well hopped pale ale and rebuilt it around American hops: Cascade, Centennial, Simcoe, Citra and their relatives. These hops smell of grapefruit, orange peel, pine and resin. The brewers used plenty of them in the kettle and again after fermentation.  The beer is gold to light amber and clear. Malt is a backdrop, a little bread and light caramel, just enough to carry the hops. Bitterness is firm and the finish is dry, which is what makes you want the next sip. A good one smells like you have just cut open a grapefruit in a pine forest. A tired one smells of cardboard and onion, because hop aroma fades fast.  The style spans a range. The West Coast version is the driest and most bitter. Others carry more malt. What they share is clarity and a bitter backbone, which is the clearest line between this and a hazy New England IPA. Drink it young and cold. Check the packaging date.

t: English IPA
d: The original IPA: earthy, biscuity and bitter, with no citrus fireworks.
x: English IPA is the older branch of the family, the strong, well hopped pale ale that British brewers sent out to India in the nineteenth century. The story of IPA being invented for the voyage is mostly legend; strong, hoppy beers kept well. That made them good for export.  What you taste is English hops: Fuggles, East Kent Goldings, Challenger. They give earth, herbs, a little black tea and marmalade, never the grapefruit of the American version. Underneath sits biscuit and toast from British pale malt, often with a touch of caramel. The yeast adds soft fruit, pear or apricot. Bitterness is firm but rounder than in an American IPA. The finish is dry with a bready echo.  It is a balanced beer by modern standards. If American IPA is a shout, this is a firm conversation. Hard water helps, which is why brewers add gypsum to make the bitterness crisp.

t: Imperial IPA
d: An IPA with everything doubled, made dry enough that you forget how strong it is.
x: Imperial IPA, also called double IPA, is what happened when American brewers asked how far an IPA could go. More malt in the mash gives more alcohol, usually 8 to 10 per cent. That alcohol needs far more hops to balance it. The result is a beer with intense aroma: grapefruit, mango, pine, resin, sometimes a dank, green note.  The skill is in keeping it drinkable. A good one is pale and surprisingly dry, because brewers use simple sugar for part of the malt and mash for fermentability so the body does not turn syrupy. The bitterness is high, but the alcohol warms and rounds it. A poor one is sticky, hot and harsh, like hop flavoured cough syrup.  Treat it as a sipping beer. Use a smaller glass, let it warm a little and share the bottle. Freshness matters even more than with a standard IPA, because there is more hop aroma to lose.

t: New England IPA
d: Hazy, soft and juicy: all the hop fruit, very little of the bite.
x: New England IPA, often just called hazy, turned the IPA idea around. Instead of bitterness, it chases hop aroma and a soft, almost fluffy body. Brewers add most hops late, in the whirlpool and as heavy dry hops, often while the beer is still fermenting. Oats and wheat in the grist add body and help keep the beer cloudy.  It looks like orange juice. It smells a bit like it too: mango, passion fruit, peach, citrus pith. Bitterness is low, so the beer reads as juicy rather than sharp. The yeast is usually a fruity English type that adds stone fruit to the hop character.  The haze is the style, but haze alone does not make it good. A fresh hazy is bright and fruity. An old one goes dull, sweet and slightly onion like. The colour darkens toward brown as it oxidises. No beer style punishes age and heat faster, so it is a beer to drink close to the brewery.

t: American Amber Ale
d: A pale ale with more caramel in the middle, built for the dinner table.
x: American amber sits between an American pale ale and a brown ale. It takes the pale ale's American hops (citrus, pine and flowers) and puts them on a deeper malt base with real caramel and toast. The colour is amber to copper and the beer is clear.  Balance is the point. Neither side wins. You get toffee and toasted bread first, then orange peel and pine, then a moderate bitterness that keeps the caramel from going sticky. Some brewers push the hops toward a red IPA; others keep it mellow. Both are fair as long as the malt stays in the picture.  It is an easy style to make dull. Too much crystal malt and it turns sweet and heavy; too little and it is a pale ale with food colouring. A good one is clean with no butterscotch and dry enough that the caramel reads as flavour rather than sugar. Put it next to dinner and it earns its place.

t: American Pale Ale
d: The beer that taught a generation what American hops smell like, at a strength you can drink twice.
x: Pour one and the hops arrive first: grapefruit peel, orange, a bit of pine, sometimes a floral edge. Underneath sits a pale, biscuity malt base with a touch of caramel, enough to carry the bitterness without turning sweet. The finish is dry and firm. It should leave you wanting a second sip rather than a glass of water.  The style took shape in California around 1980, when small brewers started using Cascade, a then-new American hop, in a beer built on the English pale ale template. Swap the earthy English hops for loud citrus ones, swap the fruity English yeast for a clean American strain and you have it. Later hops such as Centennial, Citra and Simcoe pushed it further towards tropical fruit.  What keeps it distinct from an IPA is restraint. It is lighter in alcohol, lighter in bitterness and more balanced, so the malt still has a say. A good one is the beer you order when you want flavour but plan to stay a while.

t: Blonde Ale
d: The friendly ale. Light, bready and quietly made, it is often the beer a brewpub sells most of.
x: Blonde ale is pale, soft and easy. The malt gives a light bready or crackery sweetness, sometimes a hint of honey. The hops sit in the background with a little floral or citrus lift. Bitterness is gentle. The finish is clean and fairly dry, so it never cloys.  It grew up in American brewpubs, where brewers needed an ale for customers who mostly drank lager. Fermented warm with a clean ale yeast, it is quicker to make than a lager and can be on tap in a couple of weeks, yet it drinks almost as crisply. Some brewers use a German or Czech pilsner malt for a slightly richer bread note, others add a touch of wheat for a fuller head.  There is nothing loud about it. That is the point. A blonde ale shows whether a brewer can make a clean beer with nowhere to hide. Any off note, a whiff of butter from diacetyl or a solvent edge from a hot ferment, stands out straight away in a beer this light.

t: English Bitter
d: Britain's everyday pub ale: low in alcohol, big on biscuit and earth, made for drinking slowly.
x: Despite the name, an ordinary bitter is not very bitter by modern standards. What you taste is balance: biscuit and toffee from British pale and crystal malts, an earthy, woody, sometimes marmalade-like note from English hops such as Fuggle and East Kent Goldings and a light fruitiness from English ale yeast. It is usually under 4% alcohol, so the flavour has to come from good malt and careful fermentation rather than strength.  The name came about in English pubs in the nineteenth century, when drinkers wanted to tell the paler, hoppier draught beer apart from mild. Traditionally it is served from the cask, naturally conditioned, pulled by hand pump at cellar temperature with low carbonation. That soft texture is a large part of its character.  Bitter is a family of strengths. The ordinary version is the lightest, best bitter sits in the middle and the strongest ones are sold as ESB. All share the same malt and hop backbone. All are built for a long session over conversation.

t: English Pale Ale (ESB)
d: The bitter with its sleeves rolled up: more malt, more fruit and more strength, still balanced.
x: An ESB, or extra special bitter, is the strongest member of the bitter family. It pours amber to copper and leads with malt: toffee, toast, a little caramel and a nutty biscuit note. English hops answer with earthy, woody and slightly spicy character. The bitterness is firm enough to keep all that malt in check. English ale yeast adds red apple, pear or a faint marmalade fruitiness.  The name comes from a London brewery that launched its own Extra Special Bitter in the early 1970s; the term later spread into a style category. American brewers took it up as a name for any strong, malty English-type pale ale. Compared with an American pale ale, the hops here are quieter and earthier and the malt is richer, so the beer tastes rounder rather than sharper.  Brewers often aim for a sulphate-rich water profile like Burton upon Trent's, which gives the bitterness a dry, clean edge. Get the yeast and the water right and the beer tastes deeper than its strength suggests.

t: American Lager
d: Pale, fizzy and very cold. Easy to sneer at, hard to brew well and closer to Indian beer than you might think.
x: American lager is about refreshment more than flavour. It pours very pale, with a bright white head and a lot of bubbles. The taste is a faint grainy sweetness, sometimes a hint of corn or rice, with very little hop aroma and only light bitterness. It finishes crisp, dry and clean.  The style came from German immigrant brewers in the United States in the nineteenth century. American six-row barley was high in protein and made hazy beer, so brewers thinned it with corn or rice. The result was lighter in body and colour than the lagers of Europe. It suited a hot climate and a mass market. It became the most sold beer style in the world.  Do not mistake simple for easy. With almost no malt or hop flavour to hide behind, any fault shows: sulphur, butter, cardboard from oxidation, green apple from a rushed lager. Producing it consistently at scale takes a well-run brewery, cold fermentation and a long, cold conditioning period.

t: Czech Pilsner
d: The original golden lager: richer and rounder than the German version, with Saaz spice over bread and honey.
x: The first golden lager was brewed in Plzen, in Bohemia, in 1842. The Czech version is still the fullest of the pilsners. It pours deep gold with a dense, creamy white head. The malt leads with fresh bread, a little honey and a toasted biscuit note, richer than you expect from such a pale beer. Saaz hops bring a soft spicy, herbal and floral aroma. The bitterness is clear and lasting but never harsh.  Three things make it. Very soft water lets brewers use plenty of hops without a rough edge. Floor-malted Moravian barley, often taken through a traditional decoction mash, gives it depth of malt. A Czech lager yeast can leave a trace of diacetyl, a faint butter note that is tolerated here where it would be a fault elsewhere.  Compared with a German pilsner it is rounder, sweeter and a shade darker, with a fuller body. The bitterness is just as firm, but it is cushioned rather than sharp.

t: Dortmunder Export
d: The steelworkers' lager: fuller than helles, softer than pilsner, made for a real thirst.
x: Export sits between a helles and a pilsner and is a little stronger than both. It pours gold, clear, with a white head. The malt is fuller than in a pilsner, with bread, light grain sweetness and a touch of toast. Hops are noble German types, giving a moderate floral and spicy note and a firm but smooth bitterness. The finish is drier than a helles, with a faint mineral edge.  The style is tied to Dortmund in the second half of the nineteenth century, when coal mines and steelworks gave the city a large, thirsty workforce. Dortmund water is hard, rich in sulphate, chloride and carbonate. That mineral content shapes the beer's firm, slightly salty finish. Brewers made it stronger than their everyday lager so it could stand up to shipping, which is how it earned the name.  Its fortunes faded as pilsner took over Germany. It is now uncommon even in its home city. When you find one, it is a satisfying beer: full enough to be interesting, clean enough to drink by the litre.

t: Munich Helles
d: Munich's everyday golden lager. Soft, bready and dangerously easy, it is all about the malt.
x: Helles means pale or light. Munich brewers created it in the 1890s to answer the pilsners coming in from Bohemia. Where pilsner leads with hops, helles leads with malt. The first sip is soft fresh bread, a little grainy sweetness and maybe a touch of honey. Noble hops are present only as a light floral or herbal note. The bitterness is just enough to keep the beer from tasting sweet.  Munich water is moderately hard with carbonate, which favours malt and makes a heavily hopped beer taste harsh. That is part of why the city's brewers went soft and malty. Good helles is lagered cold for weeks until it is brilliantly clear and very smooth.  It looks simple and is not. With low bitterness and pale malt there is no cover for faults: sulphur, a trace of diacetyl or a stale note from old malt will show. The best ones taste like good bread in liquid form. They are meant to be drunk by the litre in a beer garden.

t: German Pilsner
d: The crisp, dry pilsner. Lighter and more bitter than the Czech original, with a finish that snaps shut.
x: A German pilsner is pale straw to light gold and brilliantly clear, with a tight white head. On the nose it is floral and herbal from German noble hops, with a light cracker and bread malt underneath. The palate is lean. The bitterness comes early and stays firm. The finish is dry, crisp and slightly minerally.  German brewers adopted the golden lager from Bohemia in the late nineteenth century and made it their own. They used German malt and hops such as Hallertau, Tettnang and Spalt. Many breweries had harder water than Plzen. The result was a lighter-bodied, drier and more bitter beer than its Czech parent. In the north of Germany the pilsners tend to be especially dry and bitter, while southern versions are a touch softer.  It is a demanding beer to make. Highly fermentable worts, careful hop additions and weeks of cold lagering are needed for that clean, bright snap. Any haze, sulphur or butter is a fault here. Drinkers who know the style will spot it.

t: Imperial Porter
d: Porter scaled up: more chocolate, more roast, more warmth. A beer to sip, not to quench.
x: An imperial porter pours black, often with a dark tan head. The malt does most of the work: dark chocolate, cocoa, coffee, toffee and dark fruit such as raisin or plum, with some roast, though usually less burnt and harsh than an imperial stout. The alcohol, often 8% or more, shows as a gentle warmth and adds to the impression of richness. Hops are mostly there to balance, though American brewers sometimes add noticeable hop aroma.  It belongs to the American craft habit of taking a classic style and making it bigger. Porter began in eighteenth-century London as a dark, everyday beer. Strong versions were brewed for export then too. Today's American imperial porter is generally an ale, which separates it from the lager-fermented Baltic porter, its close cousin. Many brewers age it on coffee, vanilla, cocoa or in spirit barrels.  The difference from imperial stout is a matter of degree. Porter usually leans more on chocolate and less on the acrid roast of roasted barley, so it can feel smoother and slightly sweeter.

t: Baltic Porter
d: A porter that went north, swapped to lager yeast and came back strong, dark and very smooth.
x: Think of Baltic porter as the cold-climate cousin of the London porters that sailed into the Baltic in the 1700s and 1800s. Brewers in Poland, Finland, Estonia and Russia took the idea, raised the strength and, from the late 1800s, began fermenting it with lager yeast and conditioning it cold for weeks or months. That long, cold rest is the whole personality of the beer.  In the glass you get dark fruit first: plum, prune, raisin, sometimes cherry. Behind that sits toffee, molasses and a little cocoa, with roast kept on a short lead so it never turns burnt or acrid. Alcohol is there, often around 8 to 9 percent, but a good one hides it behind a smooth, almost silky body. Hops are a background job, enough bitterness to stop the sweetness cloying and no more.  What makes it itself is cleanliness. An imperial stout shouts roast and fruity ale esters. A Baltic porter is quieter and rounder, because the lager yeast leaves almost nothing behind except malt.

t: English Brown Porter
d: The original working beer of London: brown, soft, chocolatey and easy to keep drinking.
x: Porter was London's everyday beer in the 1700s, named for the street and river porters who drank it. The modern English brown porter is the gentler descendant of that beer: dark brown, moderate in strength and built around chocolate and caramel rather than sharp roast.  Take a sip and you should find milk chocolate, toffee, a little nuttiness and some bready malt. English yeast adds a light fruitiness, a hint of plum or pear. Bitterness is moderate and earthy from English hops, there to keep it dry enough for a second pint. Roast is a whisper. If it tastes like coffee grounds, it has wandered into stout or robust porter.  The point of the style is balance at a sensible strength, usually 4.5 to 6 percent. It is the dark beer you can drink through a long conversation without your palate getting tired. Brewed well, it shows how much flavour a brewer can draw from malt without leaning on alcohol or hops.

t: Robust Porter
d: Porter with its sleeves rolled up: more roast, more bitterness, still not quite a stout.
x: Robust porter is largely an American craft brewing take on the old London style. Brewers kept the chocolate backbone of porter and pushed everything a notch further: more dark malt, more hop bitterness, a little more strength. The result sits in the space between a brown porter and a stout. The border is genuinely blurry.  Expect dark chocolate and coffee first, then caramel and some bready sweetness underneath. Roast is clear but should stay on the chocolate side of burnt. Hops show as firm bitterness and, in American versions, a light piney or resinous note. Alcohol is usually 5 to 6.5 percent, so it has weight without being a sipping beer.  How do you tell it from a stout? Roughly, porter leans on chocolate malt and stout leans on roasted barley, which gives a drier, more coffee-ash edge. In practice, judge the beer in front of you. If the roast tastes like espresso and the body is fuller and drier, you are close to stout territory.

t: Smoke Porter
d: Chocolate porter, a campfire and a light hand. When the smoke is balanced, nothing else tastes quite like it.
x: A smoke porter is a porter brewed with some smoked malt in the grist. Before indirect kilns, most malt picked up some smoke from wood fires, so in one sense this is an old flavour come back. The modern version took shape in American craft brewing in the late 1980s and has spread wherever brewers like a challenge.  The base is a proper porter: chocolate, caramel, a bit of roast. On top of that comes smoke. The type depends on the malt. Beechwood-smoked malt from Bamberg gives a clean, bacon-like smoke. Cherry or oak-smoked malts are softer and sweeter. Peat-smoked malt, used carefully, brings a medicinal, Islay whisky edge that can bully everything else.  The skill is proportion. The smoke should sit inside the beer and work with the chocolate, not taste like a cold ashtray. A good one smells like a fire in another room. Strength ranges widely, from a session-friendly 5 percent to bigger, warming versions near 9.

t: Scotch Ale (Wee Heavy)
d: Strong, malty and warming. The Scottish answer to cold weather, best taken slowly.
x: Wee heavy is the strong end of the Scottish brewing tradition. The name comes from small bottles of heavy, strong ale. Scotland's cool climate and hop shortage pushed its brewers towards malt-led beers. This style is that idea taken all the way.  In the glass it is about malt. Caramel and toffee first, then dark fruit, bread crust and sometimes a light nuttiness. Long kettle boils caramelise some of the wort, which deepens the colour and the flavour. Hop bitterness is low, just enough to stop it being syrupy. Alcohol, usually 6 to 8 percent and sometimes more, shows as a gentle warmth.  A common myth: Scotch ales should taste of peat smoke. Traditional Scottish ale malt was not peated. A strong peat note is usually a brewer reaching for whisky imagery. A faint earthy note is fine. A beer that smells like a bonfire is a different style. The clean, cool fermentation keeps the focus on malt sweetness and body.

t: Scottish Ale
d: Malt-forward, low in bitterness and gentle on strength. A quiet beer with more going on than it lets on.
x: Scottish ale covers a family of modest-strength, malt-led beers once named by shillings: 60 shilling light, 70 shilling heavy and 80 shilling export. The numbers referred to the old price of a barrel. The higher the number, the stronger the beer. Strengths run from under 3 percent to a little over 5.  Flavour is about malt, not hops. Expect caramel, toast, biscuit and a soft sweetness, with a dry, slightly roasty note at the finish from a pinch of roasted barley. Bitterness is low and hop aroma barely there. Fermentation is cool for an ale, so fruity esters stay restrained and the malt reads clean.  What gives the style its character is restraint. The lighter versions are thin on paper and yet taste full, because the malt bill is built for flavour at low gravity. If you are used to bright, hoppy pale ales, this will seem quiet at first. Give it a second glass. The caramel and toast open up as it warms a little. It becomes one of the most drinkable dark-ish beers around.

t: American Brett Beer
d: One yeast, a lot of character: farmyard, tropical fruit and a bone-dry finish, without needing to be sour.
x: Brettanomyces, Brett for short, is a slow, hardy yeast that most breweries treat as an infection. A few deliberately invite it in. An American Brett beer is any ale fermented wholly or partly with Brett. In the American craft tradition that means almost any base: pale ale, IPA, saison, stout.  Brett brings two families of flavour. One is fruity: pineapple, mango, stone fruit. The other is the famous funk: hay, leather, a barnyard note, sometimes a whiff of clove or smoke. Which side shows depends on the strain, the base beer and time. Brett also eats sugars that ordinary yeast leaves behind, so these beers often finish very dry.  Brett on its own does not make a beer sour. That needs lactic or acetic bacteria. A Brett beer can be tart, but many are not. A hoppy Brett pale ale can be fruity and dry with no acidity at all. That is the clearest line between this style and an American sour. Because the colour, bitterness and strength depend on the base, the numbers vary freely.

t: American Sour
d: The broadest sour family: acidity from bacteria, often oak and fruit, plus plenty of brewer imagination.
x: American sour is less a single recipe than a way of brewing. Brewers take almost any base beer and sour it with lactic bacteria, Lactobacillus or Pediococcus, sometimes with Brett and wild yeast as well. Some age it for months or years in oak barrels. Others sour it quickly in the kettle before boiling and fermenting it clean. Many add fruit.  The flavour spread is wide. A barrel-aged sour can taste of cherry, oak, vinegar edge and leather, layered and complex. A kettle sour is cleaner and simpler: bright, lemony, yoghurt-like tartness, often with mango or berries on top. Colour, bitterness and strength all depend on the base, so the style range is wide by design.  What links them is acidity that is meant to be there and a sense of balance. Good sours taste tart and refreshing, not harsh. Any fruit tastes like fruit rather than syrup. Sharp nail-polish or sweaty-sock notes are faults, not funk.

t: Flanders Red and Oud Bruin
d: Belgium's wine-like sour: oak, cherry, a sharp edge and caramel underneath. A beer for people who say they hate beer.
x: West Flanders in Belgium is home to red ales aged for a year or two in huge oak vats called foeders. East Flanders gives its cousin, oud bruin, the old brown, usually aged in steel rather than wood and a little sweeter and maltier. Both are blends: brewers mix young and old beer to set the balance of sweet and sour.  A Flanders red smells of black cherry, plum and red currant, with a sharp vinegar note that is part of the style, not a flaw, as long as it stays in proportion. Underneath there is caramel and a little vanilla or oak. Oud bruin swaps some of the sharpness for raisin, fig and toffee. Bitterness is low, because hops would clash with the acid.  The comparison people reach for is red wine. It is fair: fruity, tart, tannic, food-friendly. The difference is the malt backbone, which gives these beers a sweetness and body no wine has.

t: Fruit Lambic
d: Wild-fermented Brussels beer, aged on whole cherries or raspberries until the fruit and the funk become one.
x: Lambic comes from the Senne valley around Brussels, the Pajottenland. The wort is left overnight in a wide, shallow cool ship so wild yeast and bacteria from the air can settle in, then it ferments and ages in old oak barrels for months or years. Fruit lambic is that beer with whole fruit added during ageing: sour cherries for kriek, raspberries for framboise and less often peach, blackcurrant or grape.  The fruit ferments out, so a traditional fruit lambic is tart and dry, not sweet. Expect the real taste of the fruit, cherry stone and almond in a kriek, bright berry in a framboise, over a sour, funky base with hay, leather and a little oak. Aged hops are used for their preservative effect, so bitterness is almost nil. Some commercial versions are sweetened after filtering, which makes them fruitier and softer but less complex.  The best of these taste like the fruit grew in the beer.

t: Lambic and Gueuze
d: Belgium's wild-fermented wheat beer, blended young and old into something sharp, dry and very much alive.
x: Lambic comes from the Senne valley around Brussels and the Pajottenland to its west. The wort, roughly 60 per cent barley malt and 40 per cent unmalted wheat, is boiled with hops that have been aged for a year or more, until their bitterness has faded but their preservative power remains. It then cools overnight in a wide, shallow coolship open to the air. Whatever yeast and bacteria drift in start the fermentation. The beer goes into oak and is left for one to three years.  Young lambic on its own is still and sharp. Gueuze is the blend: one, two and three year old lambics mixed and bottled, so the sugars left in the young beer referment and give a fine, Champagne-like sparkle. Expect lemon, green apple and a dry, almost chalky sourness, with the leather, hay and farmyard notes of Brettanomyces underneath. Bitterness barely registers. A good gueuze tastes old and fresh at the same time, which is the reason blenders bother.

t: Contemporary Gose
d: A sour, lightly salted wheat beer that drinks like a cold nimbu soda with a backbone of grain.
x: Gose began in Goslar and became the everyday beer of Leipzig: a wheat ale soured with lactic bacteria, seasoned with coriander and brewed with water that was naturally a little salty. It almost vanished in the twentieth century. The version most brewers make today comes from the craft revival. It is quicker and cleaner than the old one. Most breweries kettle sour, holding the wort warm with Lactobacillus for a day or two until the pH drops to around 3.3 to 3.5, then boiling it to stop the bacteria before a normal ale fermentation.  The result is tart and bright, never vinegary. You should feel the salt as roundness and a slight thirst rather than taste it outright like sea water. Coriander adds a citrus, slightly floral lift. Hops sit very low so they do not clash with the acid. Many modern goses add fruit. That is where the style gets most of its variety.

t: American Black Ale
d: Looks like a stout, drinks like an IPA. The trick is getting the colour without the burnt toast.
x: Most drinkers know this beer as black IPA. The argument over that name (how can a pale ale be black?) is half the reason it gets called black ale instead. It took shape in the American Pacific Northwest and New England in the 2000s. For a few years every craft brewery seemed to have one. The idea is simple and hard to pull off: the hop load and dryness of an IPA with the colour of a porter.  The craft is in the dark malt. Ordinary roasted barley or black malt brings coffee, ash and an acrid bite that clash with resinous hops, so brewers reach for dehusked black malts such as Carafa Special, often added late in the mash or steeped cold. That gives colour and a soft cocoa note with very little roast. What you should taste is pine, citrus and resin first, a light dark-chocolate shadow second and a firm, dry bitterness on the finish.

t: Barrel-Aged Beer
d: Any beer that has spent months in wood, usually picking up some of the spirit that lived there first.
x: Barrel-aged is a method rather than a recipe. Brewers take a finished beer (most often an imperial stout, barley wine or Belgian strong ale) and rest it in oak for months. The wood gives vanilla, coconut and toast from compounds released when the staves were charred or toasted. If the cask held whisky, bourbon, rum or wine, the beer draws some of that spirit out of the wood as well. Slow oxygen pick-up through the staves rounds off harsh edges and, over time, adds dried fruit and a sherry-like note.  The base beer has to be strong enough to carry all this. A light lager in a bourbon barrel tastes of bourbon and little else. A good barrel-aged beer tastes like the beer first, with wood and spirit layered in. It warms as it goes down. The classic examples usually sit at 8 per cent or more, with low carbonation and a long, sweet and woody finish.

t: Chocolate Beer
d: A dark beer with real cocoa in it, rich enough for dessert and dry enough to want another sip.
x: Plenty of stouts and porters taste of chocolate without containing any. Chocolate malt, despite the name, is just barley kilned dark. A chocolate beer goes further and adds the real thing: cocoa nibs, cocoa powder or, now and then, actual chocolate, most often to a porter or stout whose roast already points the same way. Nibs added after fermentation, much like dry hopping, give the cleanest result, because cocoa aroma is fragile and the boil drives much of it off.  Cocoa butter is the brewer's problem. Fat kills foam, so nibs are preferred to bars. Some brewers use cold extraction to pull flavour without the oil. A good one tastes like dark chocolate, with fruit, coffee and some dryness, rather than a sweet milky drink. Strength runs from session porters to imperial stouts. Lactose or vanilla often appear alongside the cocoa to round it out.

t: Coffee Beer
d: Beer with real coffee in it, from roasty stouts to pale ales that smell like a fresh pour-over.
x: Coffee beer is any beer with coffee added. The base can be almost anything. Stout and porter are the obvious partners because dark malt already tastes of roast, but pale coffee ales, coffee lagers and even coffee sours exist. The coffee should be obvious and fresh, not a vague bitterness you have to hunt for.  How the coffee goes in matters more than which bean. Hot coffee, or beans in the boil, give stale, harsh notes. Most brewers either blend in cold brew at packaging or soak whole or coarsely ground beans in the fermented beer for a day or two, much as they would dry hop. Leave them too long and you get green, vegetal or astringent flavours. Light roasts in a pale beer show fruit and florals; dark roasts in a stout show chocolate and caramel. Either way, coffee aroma fades within weeks, so these are beers to drink young.

t: Fruit and Field Beer
d: Real fruit or vegetables in the brew, where the produce should taste picked, not poured from a syrup bottle.
x: This is a broad category: any beer brewed with fruit, or with vegetables and other field produce such as chilli, cucumber or sweet potato. The base can be a wheat beer, a pale ale, a stout or a sour. What defines it is that the added ingredient is real and recognisable. Spices and herbs have their own category. Belgian fruit lambics are judged separately too.  The brewer's main decision is when to add the fruit. In the boil it sets colour but cooks off aroma. In the fermenter, yeast eats the fruit sugar, which dries the beer and nudges the alcohol up while keeping more of the aroma. Purée, juice and whole fruit all behave differently. Pectin from cooked fruit can leave a haze. The best examples taste of fruit in season, bright and slightly tart, with the beer still holding its shape underneath. Flavoured syrup stirred in at the end usually tastes like flavoured syrup.

t: Gluten-Free Craft Beer
d: Beer brewed without barley, wheat or rye. A natural fit for a country full of millet and rice.
x: Gluten-free beer is made from grains that contain no gluten: sorghum, millet, rice, buckwheat or maize. It is a method rather than a flavour, so you will find gluten-free lagers, pale ales, IPAs and stouts. The difficulty is that barley malt does a lot of the work in normal brewing. It brings its own enzymes, a husk that forms the filter bed in the mash tun and the proteins that hold a head of foam. Without it, brewers rely on malted millet or sorghum, added enzymes and patient lautering.  Sorghum gives a tangy, slightly sour, molasses-like note that early gluten-free beers were known for. Malted millet and rice brew cleaner and lighter. Many modern versions lean on hops to carry flavour, which is why gluten-free pale ales often taste closest to their barley cousins. There is also gluten-reduced beer, brewed from barley and then treated with an enzyme. That is a different product, labelled differently from country to country. Anyone with coeliac disease should take medical advice before trying it.

t: Herb and Spice Beer
d: Beer seasoned like food, where the spice should sit in the background and never shout.
x: Before hops became standard, brewers flavoured beer with whatever grew nearby: bog myrtle, yarrow, juniper and spice from the trade routes. Herb and spice beer picks up that thread. It covers any beer with added spices, herbs, flowers, roots or leaves, from ginger and cinnamon to rosemary, rose petals or tea. Belgian witbier and the old gruit beers sit close by, though witbier is usually judged as a style of its own.  Restraint is the whole skill. Spices are far more potent than fruit. A few grams per hectolitre too many will turn a beer into cough syrup or curry. Brewers usually add them late in the boil, at whirlpool or as a tincture after fermentation and taste as they go. The best ones taste like a good beer first, with the spice adding a lift you might not name on the first sip. If the spice is the only thing you notice, the brewer went too far.

t: Honey Beer
d: Honey in the brew adds aroma and dryness more than sweetness, which surprises most people.
x: Honey beer is any beer with honey added. The first thing to know is that it rarely tastes sweet. Honey is mostly simple sugar. Yeast ferments nearly all of it, so a honey ale finishes drier and a little stronger than the same beer without it. What survives is aroma: floral, waxy, sometimes herbal, depending on the flowers the bees worked.  That is why timing matters. Honey added to the boil loses most of its perfume. Brewers who want it to show usually add it once fermentation is under way, sometimes after warming it gently to knock back wild yeast. The base is often a blonde, golden or amber ale, or a wheat beer, light enough for the honey to come through. Darker versions such as honey porters and braggots made with roughly as much honey as malt, sit at the stronger end. A good one smells of the hive and finishes clean.

t: Pumpkin Beer
d: A harvest beer where the spice rack does more talking than the pumpkin.
x: Ask most drinkers what a pumpkin beer tastes of and they will describe cinnamon, nutmeg, clove and ginger. That is fair. Pumpkin flesh gives very little flavour once it has been through a mash and a boil; what it adds is a touch of body, a faint earthy sweetness and an orange cast in the glass. The spice blend, the same one Americans put in pumpkin pie, is what people actually recognise.  The style grew up in the United States, where colonial brewers short of barley used pumpkins and squash as a source of sugar. The modern version came back with the craft movement in the 1980s and turned into an autumn ritual. Underneath, the base beer can be almost anything: an amber ale, a brown ale, a porter, even a strong ale aged in a barrel.  A good one tastes like a beer first. The malt carries toffee and biscuit, the spice sits on top as seasoning. The finish stays dry enough for a second glass. A bad one tastes like a candle shop.

t: Rye Beer
d: Rye brings a peppery snap and a slick body to almost any beer you add it to.
x: Rye is less a style than an ingredient that changes whatever it goes into. Add it to a pale ale and you get a rye pale ale; add it to an IPA and you get a rye IPA; brew a Bavarian dark wheat beer with rye instead of wheat and you have roggenbier. The common thread is a dry, slightly peppery grain flavour, a little like the crust of a dark rye loaf and a body that feels oddly full and silky for how dry the beer finishes.  That silkiness comes from gums in the grain. They are also why brewers grumble about rye. Above about 20 percent of the grist, the mash turns sticky and slow to run off. Some brewers add rice hulls or a beta glucan rest to keep it moving.  The American versions lean on hops, with citrus and pine against the spicy grain. German roggenbier leans on yeast, with banana and clove from a weizen strain. Both are worth knowing.

t: Session Beer
d: Any style, brewed light enough that the third glass tastes as good as the first.
x: A session beer is defined by strength, not flavour. The usual line is 5 percent alcohol or below. The idea is old: English drinkers spent long evenings on bitter and mild at 3.5 to 4 percent long before anyone in America called it sessionable. Today you find session IPAs, session sours, session stouts and plenty of pale ales that fit the label.  The hard part is making a light beer that does not taste thin. Brewers mash a little warmer to leave more body, use crystal or oats for texture and pack in late hops so the aroma does the work that alcohol cannot. A session IPA at 4.5 percent can smell every bit as loud as a 7 percent one, then finish dry and quick.  What you should notice is balance. Nothing dominates and nothing is hot. You do not feel tired after two. That is the whole brief.

t: Smoke Beer
d: Malt dried over a fire, giving a beer that smells like a tandoor at closing time.
x: Before kilns with indirect heat, a lot of malt picked up some smoke while drying. The town of Bamberg in Franconia kept the habit on purpose, drying barley over beechwood fires. Its rauchbier is still the reference point: a dark lager that smells of bacon and campfire but drinks smooth and malty.  Smoke beer as a category goes wider. Brewers smoke porters, stouts, wheat beers and strong ales. Some use beechwood, some cherry or oak. Peat smoked malt turns up now and then, though a little goes a long way and too much tastes medicinal. Polish grodziskie, a light smoked wheat beer, sits at the other end of the scale.  The smoke should sit in balance with the base beer. The first sip can be a shock, but by the end of the glass most drinkers find the malt sweetness and the smoke have settled into something savoury and moreish.

t: Specialty Beer
d: The open category for beers that use an ingredient or method no other style has a name for.
x: Specialty beer is the drawer for everything that does not fit elsewhere. It covers beers brewed with an unusual fermentable such as rice, honey, maple or jaggery, beers built around a spice or flower and beers made with an unusual process. Because it is a catch all, it has no single taste. A saffron lager and a 15 percent barley wine both belong.  What holds it together is a way of judging. A specialty beer should taste like a good base beer plus the thing on the label. The special ingredient should be clearly there without bullying the rest. If a brewer says tulsi, you should find tulsi. If you only find tulsi, the beer has failed.  That makes the category a playground for brewpubs. It is where you find beers made with local produce, odd sugars and family recipes. It is where a brewer shows whether they understand balance or are just chasing novelty.

t: American Imperial Stout
d: The heavyweight stout: black, strong and bitter, built to be sipped slowly over an evening.
x: Imperial stout started in eighteenth century London as a strong export stout shipped to the Baltic and, legend says, to the Russian court. American craft brewers picked it up in the 1980s and pushed every dial. Their version is black, often 9 to 12 percent, with a lot of roast and a lot more hop bitterness and aroma than the English originals.  A good one tastes of espresso, dark chocolate, burnt sugar and dried fruit, with a resinous or citrus hop edge cutting through. The alcohol should be warming, not hot or solventy. That takes a healthy pitch of yeast, careful oxygenation and patience: most need months of conditioning before the harsh edges round off.  This is also the base for a lot of barrel ageing and adjunct experiments, from bourbon barrels to coffee, vanilla and coconut. Strip those away and the plain version should still stand up on its own.

t: American Stout
d: A stout with an American accent: more roast, more hops, more alcohol than the Irish version.
x: Take a dry Irish stout, raise the strength to around 6 or 7 percent, push the roast and then hop it like an American pale ale. That is close to an American stout. It shows up in the US craft boom of the 1980s and 1990s as brewers applied their love of Cascade and Centennial to darker beers.  The roast is the backbone: coffee, dark chocolate and a slightly burnt edge. Against it, citrus and pine hops give a bright, resinous lift that you would never find in a pint of Irish stout. Bitterness is firm, often in the 40s or 50s on the IBU scale. The finish is drier than you expect for a beer this dark.  The best ones keep the two halves in balance. Too much hop and it tastes like a black IPA; too little and it is just a strong porter.

t: Oatmeal Stout
d: A gentle, silky stout where the oats are felt more than tasted.
x: Oats in beer go back centuries in Britain. Oatmeal stout as a named style appeared in the late nineteenth century, partly because oats sounded wholesome to drinkers. It faded in the twentieth century and was revived in the 1980s, after which it became a staple for craft brewers on both sides of the Atlantic.  The oats rarely give a strong flavour of their own. What they give is texture. Their proteins and beta glucans make the beer smooth, round and almost creamy, so the roast tastes softer than in a dry stout of the same strength. You get milky coffee, cocoa, a little nuttiness and a hint of grainy sweetness, with moderate bitterness to keep it honest.  It sits between dry stout and milk stout: fuller and softer than the first, less sweet than the second. Strength is usually 4 to 6 percent, which makes it an easy dark beer to drink more than one of.

t: Milk Stout
d: A soft, sweet stout that tastes like coffee with milk and sugar.
x: Milk stout gets its sweetness from lactose, the sugar in milk. Brewer's yeast cannot ferment lactose, so whatever goes into the kettle stays in the beer as sweetness and body. English brewers sold it in the early twentieth century as a nourishing drink, with advertising that would never pass today. It was a working class staple in Britain for decades.  The flavour is roast coffee and chocolate, softened by that unfermentable sugar into something like a sweetened latte or a chocolate milk for grown ups. Bitterness is low, carbonation is gentle and the strength is modest, usually 3 to 6 percent. The roast stops it from tasting like dessert in a glass.  Many modern versions add vanilla, coffee or cocoa nibs. That is fine, but a plain milk stout should still taste balanced. One practical note: lactose is a dairy sugar, so a milk stout is not suitable for vegans or anyone avoiding dairy.

t: Irish Dry Stout
d: Black, light bodied and dry, with a sharp roast that is far easier to drink than it looks.
x: Irish dry stout is the beer most people picture when they hear the word stout. It is lighter than it looks. Most are around 4 to 4.5 percent, with a body closer to a bitter than a strong ale. The black colour and sharp coffee bite come from roasted barley, unmalted grain roasted until almost charred, which gives a dry, slightly acrid edge that defines the style.  It grew out of London porter, which Dublin brewers adapted in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries until it became their own. Flaked barley in the grist helps the head. Many breweries pour it on nitrogen, which gives the slow cascade and the thick, creamy collar of foam.  Drink one and look for coffee without the milk, a firm but not harsh bitterness and a quick, dry finish. Nothing should be sweet or heavy. It is a beer for long conversations.

t: American Barley Wine
d: A sipping beer with the malt of a fruitcake and the hop bite of a double IPA, built to age.
x: Pour one and it smells of toffee, dried fruit and pine resin at the same time. The malt is dense, like caramelised sugar on bread crust. The hops push back hard with grapefruit, resin and a long bitter finish. Alcohol shows up as warmth in the chest rather than heat on the tongue, at least in a well made one.  The British drank strong barley wines long before Americans did. When US brewers took the idea up in the 1970s and 1980s they kept the big grist and swapped in their own citrusy, piney hop varieties, at much higher rates. That is the difference you taste: the British version leans on malt and age, the American one makes the hops shout.  Fresh, it is bitter and bright. After a year in a cool cellar the hops fade, the malt turns to sherry and dried fig and the beer gets rounder. Many drinkers keep a few bottles back for exactly that reason. Serve it in small pours; this is a beer for the last hour of the evening.

t: American Imperial Red Ale
d: A double IPA dressed in red: heavier caramel, the same loud hops and a lot more alcohol than it looks.
x: Think of an American amber ale and turn every dial up. The colour is a deep red that glows in a window, the malt tastes of toffee and lightly toasted bread and the hops come in hard with citrus peel, pine and sometimes tropical fruit. The bitterness is high. It needs to be, because there is a lot of sugar to balance.  The style grew up in American craft brewing in the 2000s, when brewers making double IPAs wanted a version with more malt on the palate. Crystal malts give the colour and sweetness. A little roasted barley or dark crystal pushes the red without adding coffee notes. The yeast stays clean so the malt and hops do the talking.  What separates it from a barley wine is focus. An imperial red is usually a little lighter in strength and meant to be drunk fresh, with the hops at their brightest. Leave it a year and the hops fade, which helps a barley wine but mostly hurts this.

t: British Barley Wine
d: The original strong ale for slow evenings: malt, dried fruit and age, with the hops kept in their place.
x: English brewers have made very strong ales for centuries. The name barley wine stuck in the late 1800s once brewers started selling them as a match for port and sherry. Dark gold to deep amber, it tastes of malt first: bread crust, toffee, dark honey, raisin and plum. English hops add an earthy, slightly spicy bitterness, but they are there to balance, not to lead.  Fermentation with English ale yeast leaves fruity esters. In an older bottle you get notes of sherry, leather and treacle as the beer slowly oxidises. That ageing is the point. A young British barley wine can taste hot and sweet; two or three years later it is often far more rounded.  Compared with the American take, it carries less bitterness and almost none of that citrus or pine. Drink it slowly, like a dessert wine, in a small glass that lets it warm a little in your hand.

t: English Old Ale
d: A strong ale with a bit of age on it: toffee, dark fruit and a soft, vinous edge.
x: Old ale is named for what used to happen to it. English brewers kept strong beer in wooden vats for months, sometimes years. It picked up a slightly tart, vinous character on the way. Publicans then blended this stock ale with fresh beer. Today most old ales are aged for a shorter time, but the idea of a malty, warming ale with some maturity still holds.  Expect toffee, molasses, dark bread and dried fruit, with English hops quietly balancing the malt. Some examples show a light sourness or a woody note from barrel ageing; others are clean and sweet. The colour runs from amber to near black, which is why the range is so wide.  It sits below a barley wine in strength and body, so it is easier to finish a whole glass. Many breweries in Britain sell it as a winter warmer. It is often what you get when a brewer says the beer is best kept for a year.

t: American Wheat
d: Wheat beer with the banana and clove taken out: soft, bready, lightly hoppy and easy.
x: If you have had a German hefeweizen, this is the beer that looks similar and tastes quite different. American brewers use a big share of wheat malt for the soft body and pale haze, but ferment with a clean ale yeast. So there is no banana, no clove, just bread dough, a little honey and whatever the hops bring.  That hop character can be gentle and floral or quite citrusy, depending on the brewery. Bitterness stays low to moderate. Some versions are filtered and clear, others left hazy; both are fine.  The style became common in American brewpubs in the 1980s and 1990s as a friendly first craft beer. It plays that role well. It is often the base for fruit beers too, because a clean wheat beer does not clash with mango, watermelon or berries the way a spicy hefeweizen can.

t: American Wheat Wine
d: A barley wine that swapped half its barley for wheat: strong, soft, honeyed and surprisingly smooth.
x: Wheat wine is a modern American invention, from the craft breweries of the 1980s and 1990s that wanted a barley wine with a different texture. Half or more of the grist is wheat malt. That changes the whole beer. It feels rounder and softer, with flavours of bread, honey, biscuit and light caramel instead of the darker toffee and raisin of a barley wine.  Hopping varies a lot. Some brewers keep it restrained so the wheat leads; others add a solid dose of American hops for citrus and a firmer bitter finish. Either way the alcohol is high, so you get warmth and often notes of stone fruit or orange marmalade from fermentation.  A clean ale yeast is the norm. You should not taste banana or clove; this is not a strong hefeweizen. Many wheat wines are aged in bourbon or wine barrels, which adds vanilla and oak. Like other big beers, it rewards small pours and slow sipping.

t: Belgian Witbier
d: Hazy, spiced and bright with orange peel: the wheat beer India took to first.
x: Witbier is white beer, named for its pale, cloudy look. It comes from the farm breweries east of Brussels, around Hoegaarden. It nearly died out in the 1950s before a milkman named Pierre Celis revived it in the 1960s.  The recipe is unusual for a beer. A large share of raw, unmalted wheat and often some oats give a silky body and a haze that never settles. Dried orange peel and crushed coriander seed go in at the end of the boil. The coriander should taste citrusy and floral, not like a curry; that comes down to fresh seed and a light hand. Belgian yeast adds a peppery, slightly fruity note. There is a gentle tartness that makes it refreshing.  Bitterness is low. The finish is dry and bubbly. It is one of the easiest craft styles to like, which is why so many Indian brewers made a wit their first canned beer.

t: Berliner Weisse
d: Light, tart and fizzy: Berlin's sour wheat beer, closer to nimbu pani than to a lager.
x: Berliner weisse is the lightest sour beer most people will drink. It is pale, cloudy, very bubbly and sharply tart, usually around 3 per cent alcohol. The sourness comes from lactic acid bacteria, the same family that turns milk into curd, working alongside a normal ale yeast.  Berlin brewed it in huge numbers in the nineteenth century. The old way to drink it was with a dash of raspberry or woodruff syrup to soften the acid. Purists drink it plain. Hops barely register; the beer is about the clean, lemony sourness and a bready wheat note underneath.  Modern brewers usually kettle sour it, letting Lactobacillus work on the wort for a day or two before the boil. Older versions were sometimes fermented with Brettanomyces too, which adds a dry, slightly funky edge. A good one is bracing for the first sip and then very hard to stop drinking.

t: German Dunkelweizen
d: A hefeweizen in a brown coat: banana and clove over toasted bread and a little cocoa.
x: Dunkel means dark. That is the only real change from a hefeweizen. The same Bavarian weizen yeast is at work, so you still get banana, clove and sometimes a hint of bubblegum. What is new is the malt: Munich malt, dark wheat malt and a touch of caramel or roasted malt bring bread crust, toffee, nuts and faint chocolate.  Those two sides meet in a way that reminds people of banana bread, which is the most common description and a fair one. The roast should stay gentle. A dunkelweizen is never as roasty as a porter. Bitterness is low.  Most Bavarian wheat beer breweries make a dark one alongside their pale hefeweizen. It is a good choice for anyone who likes wheat beer but wants something with more depth on a cooler evening.

t: German Hefeweizen
d: Cloudy, fizzy Bavarian wheat beer where the yeast does the talking: banana, clove and fresh bread.
x: Hefe means yeast and weizen means wheat, which describes the beer exactly. At least half the grist is wheat malt. The beer is served with its yeast, so it pours cloudy with a tall white head. All the fruit and spice comes from a special Bavarian yeast strain, not from anything added.  That yeast makes isoamyl acetate, which smells of banana. It also makes 4-vinyl guaiacol, which smells of clove. The brewer steers the balance with fermentation temperature and pitching rate: warmer and lighter on yeast pushes banana, cooler pushes clove. A good one has both, with a soft bread note from the wheat and almost no hop bitterness.  Bavarians drink it at lunch, with white sausage and pretzels. It is one of the most consistent styles in the world. It also has a short shelf life. Those delicate esters fade after a few weeks, so fresh really is best.
